lessons.title: Access control in the cloud and in hybrid environments
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a cloud linked to a small building by a bridge, with an identity card lying in the middle of the bridge.
objectives: Apply the shared responsibility model to access control.
Explain identity federation and conditional access between on-premises and cloud.
Name the control tools: CASB, CSPM, CIEM, just-in-time privileged access.
Monitor access: cloud audit logs, access reviews, behavioral alerts.

references.title: NIST SP 800-210, General Access Control Guidance for Cloud Systems (2020)

blocks.text: Identity becomes the perimeter

In the cloud, resources are no longer behind the company firewall: they can be reached from the Internet, and identity decides who accesses them. A single access key forgotten in a code repository or an administration account without strong authentication is enough to expose everything.

rows: Systems, applications, data, identities and rights
Plus the operating system and runtime environment
Data, user accounts, rights and configuration

blocks.title: Identities stay with the customer
blocks.text: Whatever the model, managing accounts, rights and their review remains the customer's responsibility. Most cloud leaks come from configuration errors or overly broad rights, not from a flaw at the provider.
Linking on-premises and cloud

blocks.title: Identity federation (fédération d'identités)
blocks.text: The company's identity provider (IdP) authenticates the user, then passes an assertion to the cloud service using SAML or OpenID Connect. The user has only one account, and disabling it in the directory also cuts access to the cloud.

blocks.title: Conditional access (accès conditionnel)
blocks.text: Rule that grants, denies or tightens access according to context: managed device or not, country, risk level of the sign-in. Example: multi-factor authentication required outside the company network.

blocks.title: A federated sign-in
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: the user opens the cloud application; they are redirected to the company's identity provider; it checks identity and context (multi-factor, device); it returns a signed assertion; the application grants the rights planned for that role.

blocks.text: The control tools

rows: See and control the use of cloud services, including unapproved ones (shadow IT)
Detect configuration errors: public storage, open ports, disabled logs
Spot excessive or unused rights of people and services
Grant an administration role for a limited time, after approval

blocks.title: Workload identity (identité de charge de travail)
blocks.text: Identity assigned to an application or a service (not to a person) to access other resources. Managed identities, with automatically rotated secrets, are preferred over permanent access keys copied into code.
Monitoring access

blocks.title: Access monitoring
items: Enable and centralize cloud audit logs (sign-ins, rights changes, key creation) in the SIEM.
Alert on suspicious signals: sign-in from an unusual country, "impossible travel", creation of an administration account, disabling of logging.
Review rights regularly with business owners and remove those no longer used.
Protect emergency ("break glass") accounts: few in number, monitored and tested.

blocks.text: Exam reflex: in the cloud, the customer remains responsible for identities, rights and data. The provider secures the infrastructure it manages.

blocks.title: SOC case: an access key published by mistake
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: in the lab, a fictitious access key for a test cloud account is pushed to a public code repository. The audit logs show calls from an unknown address a few minutes later. The analyst disables the key, lists the actions performed with it, checks that no resource was created and recommends replacing permanent keys with managed identities.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: requires federation, multi-factor authentication and just-in-time access for cloud administration.
SOC manager: cloud audit logs must reach the SIEM, with alerts on rights changes.
Auditor: checks access reviews and the split of responsibilities set out in the contract.
Risk manager: considers configuration error the top cloud risk.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Shared responsibility: identities and data always stay with the customer.
CASB: use of cloud services; CSPM: configuration; CIEM: rights.
Federation passes an assertion; the cloud service does not see the password.
A permanent access key in code is a major risk: prefer managed identities.
In the cloud, identity is the perimeter.
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: the customer keeps identities, rights and data.
Federation (SAML, OpenID Connect) and conditional access link on-premises and cloud.
CASB, CSPM, CIEM, just-in-time access, managed identities.
Audit logs to the SIEM, alerts, access reviews.

lessons.title: Data storage architectures and strategies
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of three shelves: a disk array, a filing cabinet and a bucket full of small labeled objects.
objectives: Tell apart direct-attached storage, network-attached storage (NAS), storage area network (SAN) and object storage.
Name the protections specific to SANs: zoning and LUN masking.
Choose between synchronous and asynchronous replication, snapshot and backup.
Secure storage: encryption, administration, immutability, public exposure.

references.title: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure (2020)

blocks.text: Where does the data live?
Storage is not just disks: it is an infrastructure with its networks, administration consoles and copies. Attackers know it: ransomware first tries to destroy backups and snapshots before encrypting.

rows: Disk connected to a single server
No sharing; loss if the server fails
Rights on shares, encryption of exchanges
Blocks, over Fibre Channel or iSCSI
Objects in buckets, through a web API

blocks.title: Zoning and LUN masking (zonage et masquage de LUN)
blocks.text: In a SAN, zoning limits which servers see which storage ports; LUN masking limits which servers see which logical volumes (LUNs). Together, they prevent a server from reading another server's volumes.
Copying data: the right tools

rows: Each write is confirmed on both sites
Limited distance, latency; also replicates errors
Some data lost in a disaster
Image of the volume at a point in time, very fast
Often on the same device: it is not a backup
Separate copy, kept according to a policy
Must be tested and protected (offline or immutable)

blocks.title: Replication is not backup
blocks.text: Replication also copies deletions and files encrypted by ransomware. Only a separate backup, with several versions and an offline or immutable copy, lets you go back.

blocks.title: Storage tiers
blocks.alt: Three-step diagram: hot storage, fast and expensive, for data used every day; warm storage for less frequently accessed data; archive, slow and inexpensive, for long-term retention and compliance.

nodes.label: Archive
nodes.detail: tape or cloud archive, long-term retention

blocks.text: Securing the storage infrastructure

blocks.title: The key measures (NIST SP 800-209)
items: Isolate storage administration consoles and require multi-factor authentication.
Encrypt data at rest and manage keys separately, so they can be destroyed at end of life.
Keep at least one immutable (WORM) or offline copy of backups.
Regularly check that no object storage bucket is public without a reason.
Log sensitive operations: snapshot deletion, retention changes, access creation.

blocks.text: In the exam: NAS = files; SAN = blocks; object = web API and buckets. Zoning and LUN masking are the access controls of the SAN.

blocks.title: SOC case: snapshots deleted in the middle of the night
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: at 3 a.m., the logs of a fictitious storage array in the lab show the deletion of all snapshots by an administration account. The analyst recognizes a classic sign of ransomware preparation, isolates the account, alerts the response team and checks that the immutable backup copy is intact.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: requires an immutable or offline copy and separate storage administration accounts.
SOC manager: snapshot deletion or retention changes must trigger a priority alert.
Auditor: checks restore tests, not just the existence of backups.
Risk manager: chooses synchronous or asynchronous according to acceptable data loss (RPO) and the distance between sites.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: NAS: files (SMB, NFS); SAN: blocks (Fibre Channel, iSCSI).
A snapshot on the same device is not a backup.
Replication also copies errors and ransomware encryption.
Synchronous replication: no loss, but limited distance; asynchronous: small loss possible.
DAS, NAS, SAN, object: four ways to store, four attack surfaces.
SAN: zoning and LUN masking.
Replication, snapshots and backups do not protect in the same way.
Encryption, isolated administration, immutable copy, non-public buckets, logging.

lessons.title: Telephony: from the telephone network to voice over IP
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of an old rotary phone connected by a wire to a modern IP phone, with a small padlock on the wire.
objectives: Describe the public switched telephone network, the private branch exchange (PBX) and voice over IP.
Recognize the attacks: toll fraud, eavesdropping, caller ID spoofing, vishing, denial of service.
Name the SIP and RTP protocols and their secure versions.
Apply the measures: separate voice network, encryption, session border controller, PBX hardening.

references.title: NIST SP 800-58, Security Considerations for Voice Over IP Systems

blocks.text: Why telephony remains a security topic

Voice today almost always travels over IP networks. It therefore inherits network attacks, while keeping risks specific to the telephone: hijacked premium-rate calls, spoofed numbers, manipulation by voice. A poorly protected PBX can cost a fortune in a single night.

rows: Eavesdropping on the line, old signaling
Premium-rate call fraud, forgotten maintenance access
All network attacks, plus eavesdropping on the streams
Default codes, listening to sensitive messages

blocks.text: A bit of history: phreaking

In the 1960s and 1970s, "phreakers" hijacked the telephone network by whistling a 2,600 Hz tone that was also used to control the switches: signaling traveled in the same channel as the voice (in-band signaling). Operators then separated signaling from voice (out-of-band signaling, SS7). SS7 has its own weaknesses: it was designed for a closed, trusted network and, if poorly filtered, makes it possible to locate a subscriber or intercept SMS messages.

blocks.title: War dialing
blocks.text: Automatically calling series of numbers to find modems or forgotten maintenance access. It is the ancestor of port scanning.
Voice over IP

rows: Set up, modify and end calls (signaling), port 5060

blocks.title: Protecting a voice over IP call
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: the IP phone is placed in a separate voice network; SIP signaling goes over TLS; voice goes over SRTP; a session border controller (SBC) filters exchanges with the operator.

blocks.text: The attacks to know

rows: Using the PBX to place premium-rate or international calls at the company's expense
Displaying a fake caller number, for example the bank's
Voice phishing; today sometimes with a cloned voice
Capturing unencrypted RTP streams and reconstructing the conversation
Flooding lines with calls, for example those of a call center
Automated advertising or malicious calls over voice over IP

blocks.title: The measures
items: Separate the voice network from the data network (voice VLAN) and filter between the two.
Encrypt signaling (SIP over TLS) and voice (SRTP).
Place a session border controller (SBC) at the edge, facing the operator.
Harden the PBX: change default codes, close maintenance access, block unneeded premium-rate destinations, monitor call volumes at night.
Train employees on vishing: call back on a known number before any sensitive action.

blocks.text: In the exam: SIP = signaling, RTP = voice; SRTP encrypts the voice. Toll fraud targets the PBX; caller ID spoofing is used for vishing. In-band signals made phreaking possible.

blocks.title: SOC case: international calls at night
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: the dashboard of the lab's fictitious PBX shows hundreds of calls to premium-rate numbers between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m., from a voicemail extension. The analyst suspects toll fraud through a voicemail code left at its default value, blocks international destinations, changes the code, and adds an alert on call volume outside business hours.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: telephony is part of the security scope; it is included in audits and tests.
SOC manager: PBX and session border controller call logs must reach the SIEM.
Auditor: checks default codes, maintenance access and the separation of the voice network.
Risk manager: toll fraud adds up fast; sets the acceptable cost limit and the related alerts.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: SIP sets up the call; RTP carries the voice.
SRTP encrypts the voice; SIP over TLS encrypts signaling.
Phreaking exploited in-band signaling (2,600 Hz).
The displayed number can be spoofed: it does not prove the caller's identity.
War dialing looks for modems; vishing manipulates a person.
PSTN, PBX, VoIP, voicemail: each has its risks.
Phreaking: in-band signaling; SS7: out-of-band signaling, to be filtered.
SIP (signaling, TLS) and RTP (voice, SRTP).
Toll fraud, caller ID spoofing, vishing, eavesdropping, TDoS, SPIT.
Voice VLAN, encryption, SBC, hardened PBX, awareness.

questions.prompt: In SaaS, who remains responsible for user accounts and rights?
questions.explanation: Whatever the model, the customer manages its identities, rights and data.

whyNot.2: It plays no part in rights.
whyNot.3: It manages the application and infrastructure, not the rights granted by the customer.

questions.prompt: What does the identity provider send to the cloud service during a federated logon?
questions.explanation: With SAML or OpenID Connect, the service receives a signed assertion and never sees the password.

whyNot.0: That is precisely what federation avoids.
whyNot.1: Only the useful information is sent.
whyNot.2: A private key never leaves its holder.

questions.prompt: Which tool detects cloud storage made public by mistake?
choices: A cloud security posture management tool (CSPM)
questions.explanation: The CSPM compares the cloud configuration with best practices and reports deviations.

whyNot.0: It controls how users use cloud services.
whyNot.3: It protects the edge of the telephony system.

questions.prompt: Requiring multifactor authentication only outside the company network falls under what?
questions.explanation: The decision depends on the context of the connection: location, device, risk.

whyNot.0: It splits an operation between two people.
whyNot.1: It is a SAN storage control.
whyNot.2: It links two identity domains, without any context rule.

questions.prompt: How should a cloud application preferably access another resource?
choices: With a key copied into the code
With an account shared by the team
questions.explanation: A managed identity renews its secrets automatically, with no permanent key to protect.

whyNot.0: A key in the code often ends up published.
whyNot.1: A shared account makes it impossible to know who is acting.

questions.prompt: Which tool spots excessive or unused rights of cloud accounts?
questions.explanation: CIEM analyzes the permissions actually used in order to apply least privilege.

whyNot.1: It detects attacks on the network.
whyNot.2: It controls the use of cloud services.
whyNot.3: It targets configuration errors in resources.

questions.prompt: Which signal in the cloud audit logs should alert the SOC?
choices: A document opened by its author
questions.explanation: An attacker often disables logging to hide their actions.

whyNot.0: An author viewing their own document is normal.
whyNot.2: Viewing a dashboard is a routine activity.
whyNot.3: An expected logon, at the usual time and from the usual place.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a NAS and a SAN?
choices: None, they are two names for the same thing
questions.explanation: The NAS shares files (SMB, NFS); the SAN provides blocks (Fibre Channel, iSCSI).

whyNot.3: It is the other way around.

questions.prompt: Which control prevents a server from seeing another server's volumes in a SAN?
questions.explanation: LUN masking limits the volumes visible to each server; zoning limits the ports.

whyNot.1: It copies writes to a second site.
whyNot.2: It moves data according to how it is used.
whyNot.3: It removes duplicates to save space.

questions.prompt: Why is a snapshot not a backup?
choices: It is always encrypted by default
It often depends on the same device
It is far too slow to create
questions.explanation: If the storage array is lost or compromised, its snapshots are too.

whyNot.2: It does allow you to return to a previous state.
whyNot.3: On the contrary, it is very fast.

questions.prompt: Why does replication not protect against ransomware?
choices: It also copies the encrypted files
questions.explanation: Replication reproduces every write, including the ransomware's; versioned, immutable backups are needed.

whyNot.0: It has no effect on the antivirus.
whyNot.3: It works between disks or storage arrays.

questions.prompt: When should synchronous replication be preferred?
choices: When no data loss is acceptable
When the sites are thousands of kilometers apart
When ten years of history must be kept
questions.explanation: Each write is confirmed on both sites: a near-zero RPO, at the cost of a limited distance.

whyNot.1: Latency makes synchronous replication hard over long distances.
whyNot.2: That is the role of archiving.
whyNot.3: On the contrary, it requires a fast link.

questions.prompt: Which risk is typical of object storage in the cloud?
choices: A bucket made public by mistake
questions.explanation: Many leaks come from buckets accessible to anyone on the Internet.

questions.prompt: Which copy best protects backups against ransomware?
choices: A snapshot on the same storage array
A network share accessible to everyone
questions.explanation: A copy that can be neither modified nor deleted remains usable after the attack.

whyNot.0: It can be deleted along with the storage array.
whyNot.3: The ransomware will be able to encrypt it too.

questions.prompt: In a voice over IP call, which protocol carries the voice?
questions.explanation: SIP sets up and ends the call; RTP carries the voice.

whyNot.1: It is used to monitor devices.

questions.prompt: Which protocol encrypts the voice of a voice over IP call?
questions.explanation: SRTP is the encrypted, authenticated version of RTP.

whyNot.3: It protects the signaling, not the voice.

questions.prompt: Hundreds of premium-rate calls go out from the PBX at night. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: The attacker uses the PBX to place expensive calls at the company's expense.

whyNot.1: It looks for modems by calling series of numbers.
whyNot.3: It floods the lines to make the service unavailable, without placing premium-rate calls.

questions.prompt: What did phreakers exploit with the 2,600 Hz tone?
choices: The Wi-Fi access of the exchanges
questions.explanation: Signaling traveled in the same channel as the voice: a well-chosen tone could control the exchange.

whyNot.0: Voice over IP appeared much later.

questions.prompt: A call displays the bank's number. What can be concluded?
choices: That the carrier has verified the caller
That the call is encrypted with SRTP
That the call really comes from the bank
Nothing: the number can be spoofed
questions.explanation: The displayed number is easy to fake; you must call back on a known number.

whyNot.1: The display has no link with encryption.

questions.prompt: Which device filters voice over IP exchanges with the carrier, at the edge of the network?
questions.explanation: For voice, the SBC plays the role of an application firewall at the edge.

whyNot.0: It connects servers to SAN storage.
whyNot.1: It controls the use of cloud services.

questions.prompt: Which TWO measures reduce the risk of toll fraud on a PBX?
choices: Switching the SAN to synchronous replication
questions.explanation: Default codes and open expensive destinations are the two doors to fraud.

whyNot.1: Storage has no link with fraud.
whyNot.2: That would be a data leak.
